reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Asher ran to the swing at the park. "Stay close to me," said Mommy. So Asher swung right next to her. The sun made the slide hot to touch. A big kid touched it and pulled his hand back fast. "Hot," said Mommy. "Let a grown-up check first." She put her hand on the slide. "Still hot. We will come back."

Soon it was time to go home. Asher was hot too. Mommy said, "Let's bring your juice for the walk." Asher sipped his cold juice. It was sweet and cool. The cold juice made his hot day feel better.

At home, Daddy ran the bath. Asher wanted to jump right in. "Wait," said Daddy. Daddy put his hand in the water. "A grown-up checks first. Warm, not hot. All good." Asher touched the water with one little toe. It was warm like a hug. He splashed and laughed. Then a rubber duck popped up from under the bubbles. "Quack!" said Asher, and he was happy.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Isaiah sat in his car seat. The car went fast. Then the car went slow. "Mama, why did we go slow?" he asked. "A big truck was in front of us," said Mama. "Now it is gone."

Mama smiled at him. "Let's play the opposite game," she said. "I say a word. You shout its opposite. Two words as different as they can be are opposites, like big and small." "Yes!" said Isaiah. "Start!"

Mama said, "Big." "Small!" said Isaiah. He won that one. Mama said, "Fast." "Slow!" said Isaiah. He laughed. His voice sounded loud in the little car.

Mama said, "Hot." Isaiah thought hard. He looked out the window. He saw a cup of ice in his hand. The ice was so cold on his fingers. "Cold!" he shouted. "You win again," said Mama. Then she stopped the car. She held his cup of warm cocoa, and blew on it. "This is hot," she said. "So sip it slow." Isaiah touched his cup with just one fingertip. The ice in his other hand stayed cold. "Ice is cold," he said. "Cocoa is hot. Opposites!" Mama buckled his seat belt again. "Ready to play more?" she asked. Isaiah grinned. "Go!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Raphael was at the dentist. The friendly nurse gave him a sticker. Then Raphael had to use the toilet. He hurried out fast. He wanted his snack.

The nurse stood by the little sink. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet," she said. Raphael looked at his hands. They looked clean. But he went back anyway.

He pushed the soap pump. Bubbles! He rubbed and rubbed. The nurse helped him count to twenty. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. The water washed the bubbles away.

Then Raphael sat in the middle of the big chair. He opened his crackers. He ate them with clean hands. The dentist peeked in and smiled. "Nice brushing too," she said. Raphael skipped to the door with his sticker.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Eva rode the school bus. It was her first day of school. She held her pink backpack on her lap. The bus went bump, bump, bump. "One stop, two stops, three stops," said the driver. "Yours is next." Eva got off with her teacher.

Outside, the playground had a big slide. Eva wanted to go down it. She ran to the steps. But other children stood in a line. One, two, three, four children waited. Eva tried to go up first. A boy said, "We take turns on the slide." So Eva went to the back.

Each child went down. Whee! One gone, two gone, three gone, four gone. Then it was Eva's turn. She slid down fast. The wind tickled her nose. A girl named Mia ran to the back. "Your turn now," Eva said, and she ran too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Arlo sat at the big table. He had paper and washable markers. He drew a red sun. He drew a green garden. One, two, three flowers in the garden.

Then the blue marker slipped. It drew a long blue line on his hand. "Oh no," said Arlo. "My hand is blue." He looked and looked. Would it stay blue forever? "I guess I will try water," he said.

Mama helped him at the sink. She turned on the water. Arlo rubbed his hand with soap. The soap felt slippery. He rubbed and rubbed. The blue line went away. All gone! Arlo held up his clean hand. "Washable markers wash off with soap and water," he said. Then he went back to the table. He drew one, two, three more flowers. "This time I will be careful," said Arlo. He smiled at his clean, wet hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Snow fell at school today. Avery looked out the window. The snow was white. "I will draw the snow," she said.

She got white paper. She drew with her white crayon. She looked and looked. She could not see the snow. "Where did it go?" she said. Her friend Mia came over. "Try blue paper," said Mia. Avery got blue paper. She was careful with the glue pot so it would not spill. She drew with her white crayon. Now the snow showed up. White on blue!

Avery drew a red hat. She drew a green tree. She drew a yellow sun. She drew her pet dog, too. He was brown with white snow on his nose. "Look," said Avery. "My snow is white, like real snow." Mia clapped her hands. The two friends hung their pictures by the window. Outside, more white snow fell down, down, down.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her tummy felt fluttery, like small wings inside.

Mom knelt down next to her. "My tummy felt that way too, on my first day," Mom said. "Feeling nervous is okay."

Elizabeth held Mom's hand. Then she saw a boy by the cubbies. His backpack had a stuck zipper. He pulled and pulled. It would not move.

Elizabeth walked over. "Can I help?" she asked. The boy nodded. She held the backpack still. He pulled the zipper again. This time it slid open. A slimy toy frog jumped out and landed on the floor. They both laughed.

"I am Sam," the boy said. "I am Elizabeth." The teacher rang a soft bell. Time for a story on the rug.

Elizabeth sat next to Sam. Her tummy felt calm now. Mom waved from the door.

"Thank you for my frog," Sam whispered.

"Thank you for sitting with me," said Elizabeth. She opened the book about frogs and turned the first page.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Beau sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Look!" said Mom. "A cow!" "An animal!" said Beau. He saw a dog too. Another animal!

It was windy outside. The trees waved their leaves. Beau saw a store with apples. "Food!" he said. He saw a shop with balls and bears. "Toys!" said Beau. "Yes, toys," said Mom. She laughed.

Then the window was open a little. The wind blew something in. It landed on Beau's lap. It was soft. It was a feather! "Mom! Look!" said Beau. He held it up. Mom peeked in the mirror. "A bird lost that," she said. "Birds are animals that have feathers." Beau looked out the window. A bird flew by! It had feathers too. Beau waved his feather at it. "Bye, bird!" he called. "Bye!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Myles went to the airport with Dad to get her. They waited by the big doors. "Families wait here to meet people coming off a plane," said Dad. The doors opened. A man walked out. "Grandma!" yelled Myles. It was not Grandma. It was a tall man with a hat. The doors opened again. "Grandma!" It was not Grandma. It was a lady with a dog in a bag. Dad laughed. "You keep looking, Myles." The doors opened one more time. "Grandma!" It was Grandma! She gave Myles a big hug.

The next day, they went to the park. Myles ran to the swings, but the gate was closed. "Closed!" said Myles. Grandma showed him a little latch. She pushed it up, and the gate swung open. Myles ran in and did a big spring from his toes, up into the air. "Look at me!" he said. Grandma clapped and said, "Again, please!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the table. Nora wanted to draw on it, but she did not know how to start. "Watch," said Mia. Mia pressed one small button. The screen lit up. Nora pressed it too. The screen lit up again.

Mia tapped a little picture of a paint pot. A drawing app opened. Nora put her finger on the screen and slid it across. A purple line followed her finger! She moved her finger again and again. Soon she had a long squiggly line. It looked like a snake. "My snake!" said Nora. She gave it a messy tongue.

A bell rang. It was time for a snack. Nora pressed the button and the screen went dark. She set the tablet down next to Mia's book. "All done," she said. Then she ran to the table, and behind her the tablet sat quiet and neat, with a snake hidden inside.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Paisley walks to the bookmobile with her dad. It is a big blue bus full of books. Paisley wants one book very much. It is about a little red fox.

The librarian smiles at Paisley. "You can have your very own library card," she says. Paisley holds the card with two hands. It has her name on it. Paisley feels a big, happy feeling inside.

Paisley hugs the fox book to her chest. Then she sees the door of the bookmobile. "I have to put it back now," she says. Her face goes sad.

The librarian shakes her head. "No, you can take it home," she says. "Your card lets you borrow it. You can read it at home. Then you bring it back next week."

"My card lets me take the fox home?" Paisley asks. "Yes," says the librarian. "That is what a card does."

Paisley holds the card up high. "Take it home! Take it home!" she says. The card is a little rough on the edges. Paisley likes that. It feels real.

At home, Paisley puts the card in her pocket. She sits with Dad on the soft couch. They read about the little red fox. The fox finds his mom in the end.

Paisley pats her pocket. "Good card," she says. "We go back next week."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lennon went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. It was Diwali day. Little lamps sat in rows on a long table. Each lamp was small and clay. Each lamp needed a flame.

"I want to light one," said Lennon. She reached for a match on the table. Mama held her hand. "Grown-ups light the flames," said Mama. "You can pick a lamp for me." Lennon looked down the row. She chose a fat lamp with a red stripe. "This one, Mama." Mama lit it with the match. The wick made a small flame. It flickered and glowed.

The flame sent warm light onto Lennon's face. Then Mama put the lamp in the window. "The wrong place would be under the paper stars," said Papa. He moved a paper star far away. Lennon watched her lamp shine. "I picked it," she said. Mama smiled and held her hand. The little flame danced in the glass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Lucy went to the park with her dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Lucy wore her sun hat to keep the sun off her face.

Then the leaves began to move. The trees went swish, swish. "It is windy," said Dad. The wind blew hard. Lucy's hat flew right off her head!

"Oh no," said Lucy. "My hat is gone!" She ran after it on the grass. The hat rolled and tumbled. Dad ran too. He caught it by the swing.

Dad put the hat back on Lucy's head. He tied the strap under her chin. "There," he said. "Now the wind can't take it again."

Lucy patted the hat to keep it on. "Good hat," she said. A kind boy gave her a daisy from the dirt by the fence. Lucy smelled it. The wind blew her hair, but the hat stayed put.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Hailey sat at a little table in the cafe. Mom gave her a pencil and a paper napkin. "You can write your name," Mom said. Hailey wanted to write her name so much.

She held the pencil tight. She pressed down hard. Snap! The black tip broke off. The pencil had no point now. "My pencil broke," Hailey said. Mom got a new pencil from her bag. "Try again," she said. "Press soft this time."

Hailey held the pencil with soft fingers. She pressed gently. The tip stayed whole. She made a big H. Then a round a. Then i, l, e, y. There it was. Hailey! The letters were a little crooked, but Mom said they were not ugly at all. Mom kissed the top of Hailey's head. Hailey kissed the paper, right beside her name. Then she painted a small red heart under the H, with her crayon. "Now everyone knows this is mine," Hailey said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lily wants to draw a big yellow cat. Her teacher hands her a tablet. Lily takes it with one hand. The tablet tips and slips. It almost falls to the floor. Her teacher catches it just in time.

"Try again," says her teacher. "One, two, hands." Lily holds the tablet with one hand. It wobbles. Lily holds the tablet with two hands. Now it sits still and safe in her arms. She smiles and carries it to the little table.

Lily presses the round button. The screen lights up. She taps the blue square and the drawing app opens. She moves her finger on the screen. A straight line appears, then a tail, then two pointy ears. She draws a stick for the cat to scratch. The cat needs one, two, three whiskers. Lily counts them out loud.

The bell rings. Time to go. Lily presses the button and the screen goes dark. "One, two, hands," she says. She carries the tablet with two hands and sets it in the basket. "Bye, yellow cat," says Lily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted to buy apples for a snack.

Mom said, "Let's count the apples." Sarah put them in the bag, one by one. "One, two, three," she said. She found one more. "Four, five, six, seven." Two more made it nine. Then Mom held up one last apple. "Ten!" said Sarah. Ten apples in the bag.

At the sign, Sarah saw numbers. The sign said 10 beside the apples. Sarah frowned. "Why does ten have a 1 and a 0? Little numbers have just one number." Mom said, "I guess that is how ten is written. A 1, then a 0." Sarah traced the numbers with her finger. First a 1. Then a round 0. "Ten," she read. She smiled big.

On the way home, they passed the cracker boxes. Sarah spotted a triangle on one box. "Look, Mom. A triangle cracker! So cute." Mom laughed. At home, Mom washed the apples. Sarah counted them again, all the way to ten. Then she bit into the biggest one. "Ten apples make one good snack," said Mom. Sarah nodded, munching happily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ibrahim sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. He looked out of the window. He saw a big blue river. Some ducks sat by the water. "Look, ducks!" he said.

Ibrahim felt hungry. "Can I have my snack, please?" he asked. Dad reached back. He passed the little bag of crackers. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. Dad smiled at him in the mirror.

The bag had a tight top. Ibrahim pulled it. He pulled and pulled. His hands hurt a bit. The top would not open. His face went hot and cross. Then he took a big breath. He said, "Dad, it is too hard. Can you help me, please?"

Dad pulled over and stopped the car. He turned around and opened the tight top. It made a pop sound. "Here you go," said Dad. "Thank you, Dad," said Ibrahim. He ate a cracker and watched the ducks fly over the river. "This was a good early morning ride," said Dad. Ibrahim gave Dad a cracker too. "One for you," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Lydia stood on the baseball diamond. Daddy brought a purple hoop and a big red ball.

"Throw the beanbag in," said Daddy.

Lydia threw the beanbag. She thought it would bounce. It went flop. It lay still on the grass.

She picked it up. She threw it again. Flop. It fell flat and stayed down. She patted it with her hand.

"It doesn't bounce," said Lydia.

Then Lydia threw the big red ball. Bounce, bounce, bounce! The ball hopped high. But it rolled away from her hands.

"Try again," said Daddy. "Use both hands."

Lydia held out both hands. She waited. Daddy rolled the ball to her. She caught it. She hugged it tight.

Now Lydia looked at the beanbag. It would not roll away. She held it up. She let go. Flop. It fell right down into the purple hoop.

"I did it!" said Lydia.

Daddy clapped. "One more time," he said.

Lydia brought the beanbag back. She held it high. She let go. Flop. In it went, soft as a sleepy cat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Charlie ran to the table with muddy hands. "Bath first, then supper," said Mom.

"Why?" asked Charlie.

"Muddy hands make muddy bread," said Mom. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Charlie looked at her hands. They were very muddy. She had been digging at school all day. She had made a big mud pie.

So Charlie went to the sink. Mom turned on the water. Charlie washed and washed. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

Then Charlie sat at the table. Mom had baked bread, and it smelled good. Charlie picked up a piece. Her bread stayed clean.

"Look, Mom! No mud on it," said Charlie.

"You are a smart girl," said Mom.

After supper, Charlie put on her soft pajamas. She yawned a big yawn.

"Can mud pie be my breakfast?" she asked.

Mom laughed. "No, silly. Mud is for digging, not for eating."

Mom tucked Charlie into bed. Charlie closed her eyes. Her clean hands rested on the blanket.

"Goodnight, mud pie maker," Mom whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Addison went to the library for story time. The librarian, Miss Ana, held up a book. "Today's story is about shapes," she said. Addison clapped her hands.

After the story, Miss Ana put out paper shapes on the big table. There was a square. There was a triangle. There was a long rectangle. And there was a circle, round like a pancake.

"Let's make a shape house," said Miss Ana. "I will cut the shapes for you, because scissors are sharp." Addison picked up the circle. "This can be the sun," she said.

Miss Ana handed Addison the square. "You can glue this one," she said. Addison pressed the square onto the paper. Then she pressed the triangle on top, like a roof. The rectangle made a door. She scratched the glue with her finger to make it stick.

Addison looked at the circle again. She turned it over. She turned it around. "Miss Ana," she said, "I want to cut this one too, but I can't find the corner to start."

Miss Ana smiled. "That is because a circle is round and has no corners," she said.

Addison felt the edge with her finger. Round and round her finger went. "It just keeps going!" she said. She giggled. "Silly circle."

Miss Ana cut slow, careful snips around the sun. Then Addison glued it high in the sky. Her shape house had a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and one round, no-corner sun.

"Your house needs a mean old cat," said her friend Ben. "A mean triangle cat!"

"Here, kitty kitty," said Addison.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
James was painting at school. He wanted to paint green grass. He looked in the green paint pot. It was empty.

"My grass needs green," said James. He sat and thought. Then he saw a blue pot and a yellow pot.

He put blue paint on his brush. Then he put yellow paint on it too. He mixed them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Look, look!" said James.

His friend Mia came over. "Green," she said. "What is its name?" "Grass," said James. He painted tall grass and short grass. All of it was green.

Outside, the wind blew cold. The water cup felt almost frozen on his fingers. Miss Bell said, "Let's hang the paintings up to dry." They waited and waited. The paint dried slowly. Then James saw his green grass, hanging on the wall. "Blue and yellow," he said with a big smile.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Athena wanted to help cook. Her mama said, "You can wash the apples." Athena ran fast to the sink. The water splashed up. Splash, splash! Her socks got wet. Her curly hair got little drops on it too.

"Wet socks feel squishy," said Athena. She looked down at her feet. The big puddle was on the floor. The small puddle was on her sock. Mama came over slow and careful. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mama. "You need dry socks now." Athena sat on her little chair. She pulled off one wet sock. She pulled off the other wet sock. Her feet were cold and drippy.

Mama brought warm, dry socks from the basket. Athena pushed her toes in. Soft! Dry! She wiggled her toes inside them. Then Mama let Athena dry the apples with a towel. Rub, rub, rub. The apples went from wet to shiny and dry. Athena held one up to the window. It looked like a little red moon. "The apple is all dry," she said. "And me too!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Beatrice loved school. At play time, she saw Tom and Mia in the corner. They fed a toy bunny with a tiny spoon. Beatrice wanted to play too. She stood and watched. The bunny got one spoon, then two spoons, then three spoons of pretend carrots.

Beatrice did not know how to start. She held her teddy bear tight. Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend we run a bear hospital!" she said.

Tom looked up. Mia looked up. "A bear hospital!" said Mia. "I will be the doctor." Tom grabbed a blanket for a bed. Beatrice bent down and laid her teddy in it. One bandage, two bandages, three bandages on the teddy's paw. "All better," said Doctor Mia.

Just like that, the game had begun. Beatrice smiled a happy smile. She had said the magic words, and friends came running. "Let's pretend we bake a cake next!" said Tom. Beatrice clapped her hands and stirred a pretend bowl round and round.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milo ran to the block corner at school. Yesterday he had built a tall tower there. Today he wanted to build one again. But Ben was already playing with the blocks.

"You can play with the blocks later," said Miss Ana, a kind woman with a loose blue sweater.

Milo sat down at the little table. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Ana. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Milo watched Ben stack a red block, then a blue one. Ben dropped one block. It rolled under the shelf. Ben had to reach far to get it. While Ben reached, his tower wobbled. Down it fell. Blocks rolled everywhere on the soft rug.

Milo picked up a block and handed it to Ben. "Thank you," said Ben. "Do you want to help me build it now?"

"Now?" said Milo. He grinned. "Yes!"

They stacked the blocks side by side. Miss Ana came over and watched. "You two can paint together tomorrow," she said.

"Tomorrow is after later," said Milo.

"It sure is," said Miss Ana, and she put two brushes by the paint cups.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Lillian had a cold. Her nose was red. Her throat felt scratchy. She sat on the sofa with her blanket.

Grandma brought her a cup. It was a small blue cup. It had a star on it. "This is your special cup," Grandma said. "Try a little sip of water."

Lillian shook her head. "I am not thirsty," she said. Grandma put the cup in her hands anyway. Lillian took one small sip. Then she took another. The water was cool and fresh.

Grandma sat beside her. They watched a plane fly past the window. It left a long white line in the sky. Lillian sipped some more water while she watched.

Soon Lillian sat up a little taller. Her throat felt better. Her voice came back clear. "Grandma, can I have more water?" she asked. Grandma smiled and filled the little blue cup again. Lillian held it with both hands and took a big drink. Then she said, "That star cup is the best cup ever."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James was at the bank with Mom. It was cold outside. James had his red coat on his lap.

"Time to go," said Mom. James held up his coat. He put one arm in. He looked for the other sleeve. Where did it go? He turned and turned. The sleeve was hiding behind him.

A big kid named Ben was there too. Ben had a blue coat. "Watch this," said Ben. Ben laid his coat on the floor. The hood went down by his toes. Ben put his arms in the sleeves. Then Ben flipped the coat over his head. The coat was on!

Could James do that too? He laid his coat on the floor. The hood went down by his toes. He put his arms in the sleeves. He flipped it over his head. It worked! The coat was on, all by himself.

Now the zipper. James touched the zipper pull. He pushed it up, up, up. It went click, click, click. Mom smiled. "Good job, James."

On the wall was a picture of a snowman. "Look, Mom," said James. "He has a coat too." James patted his own warm coat and walked out the big door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Mohamed went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought a big round loaf of bread. They bought a jar of golden honey. At home, Mohamed wanted to make breakfast for the family. "I will make honey toast," he said.

Dad got the butter from the fridge. Mohamed poked it with his finger. The butter was hard as a little hammer. "Ouch," said Mohamed. "It will not spread!" He tried to push it on the bread. The hard butter made a hole in the soft bread. "Oh no," said Mohamed. "The bread has a loose crumb now!"

Dad smiled. "Let's set the butter on the counter," he said. "We can wait." They set the butter down. They watched a fly buzz past the window. They washed the blueberries. They sang a toast song. Mohamed poked the butter again. Now it was soft! His finger went right in, squish.

Mohamed spread the soft butter all over the bread. He drizzled the honey on top. Mom took a big bite. "Mmm," she said. "Best toast ever!" Mohamed held up his plate. "More honey, please!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Rosalie was going on a big trip. First she went to the airport. It was loud and busy. So many people! So many feet!

Then Rosalie saw the planes. Big planes in the window! "I want to run!" she said. She started to go. But the crowd was thick. Feet everywhere. Mama held out her hand. "Hold my hand in the crowd," she said. Rosalie took it. Her hand felt warm in Mama's hand. Together they walked and walked. In busy places, children stay close and hold hands. Rosalie held on tight.

At last they got to the beach. The sand was warm. The water went swish, swish. Rosalie found a tiny shell. It was pink. "Look, Mama! A tiny pink shell!" The waves came in. The waves went out. Rosalie held Mama's hand by the water. "Can we stay here all day?" she asked. Mama laughed and squeezed her hand.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai sat on Grandma's big soft rug. Grandma was humming a song. Kai wanted to sing it too. But he did not know the words yet.

Grandma clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Try it," she said. Kai clapped too. His claps were fast. Too fast! Grandma slowed down. Clap, clap, clap. Kai waited. Then he clapped with her. Now his claps were just right.

"Now sing," said Grandma. She sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Kai opened his mouth. He knew this tune! It was the same tune as his ABC song. He sang, "A, B, C, D." Grandma laughed. "Same song!" she said. Kai clapped and sang. He sang the ABC song all the way to Z. Then he sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Same tune, new words.

"You sing like a fish can swim," said Grandma. Kai clapped his hands. "Naughty song," he giggled. "It tricked me!" Grandma clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. "Sing it again," said Kai.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxon woke up at Grandma's house. The sun made a warm line on his blanket. He wanted to go outside and play in the leaves. But first he had to get dressed.

Grandma laid out his clothes. Jaxon pulled on his pants. He pulled on his shirt. Then he pushed his feet into his shoes. He tried to walk. His bare toes felt cold and bumpy inside. He laughed and sat back down on the bed.

He pulled the shoes off. He wiggled his feet into his soft blue socks first. Then he pushed his shoes back on. Now his feet felt warm and cozy. He stood up and stomped. The shoes stayed on.

Grandma was waiting at the door. "Ready for breakfast?" she asked. Jaxon ate warm oatmeal that Grandpa made at the stove. After breakfast, he ran outside. The leaves crunched under his feet. A shy little cat peeked out from behind the bench. Jaxon knocked gently on the wood. "Hello, cat," he said. "Come play with me." The cat blinked and stepped out into the sun.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jake went to the library with his mom. He saw a big wooden train table. He wanted to play with it so much. But a girl named Mia was already there. She held the long red train.

Jake reached for it. Mia pulled it back. "I had it first," she said. Jake felt like he might cry.

Then the librarian knelt down. She had a bee sticker on her sweater. "You can take turns," she said. "Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another." Mia nodded. "You first," she said to Jake. Jake pushed the red train all around the track. It went under the bridge and past the messy block tower. Then he stopped. "Your turn now, Mia," he said. Mia laughed and pushed the train fast. Jake clapped. When her turn was done, it was his go again. They played until the lights blinked. "Time to go," said Mom. Jake waved to Mia. "See you next time," he said, holding his bee sticker tight.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mason lost his monkey. It was his favorite toy. The monkey had a long tail and a spotted tummy.

"Where did it go?" Mason asked. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. He looked in Grandma's big chair. No monkey.

"Maybe it went on the bus," said Grandma. "You took the bus yesterday." They walked to the bus stop. The bus driver smiled. He held up the monkey!

"This tag says Mason," the driver said. "So I knew it was yours." Grandma had written Mason's name on the tag.

"How does the tag know me?" Mason asked. He looked at the little letters. M for Mason. The letters spelled his name.

"Let's look for more tags," said Grandma. They went back inside. They wrote Mason's name on his toy truck. They wrote it on his red ball. They even wrote it on a block they used to build a tower.

"One name, two names, three names," said Mason. Every toy got a tag.

Then Mason hugged his monkey tight. "Now everyone knows you are mine," he said. "My name is on your tag!"

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find the letter M. Her teddy bear had a tag with an M on it. But she did not know where M lived.

The library had a big rug with letters on it. Brooklyn sat down on the A. "A says ah," she said. Dad smiled. She hopped to B. "B says buh," she said. She hopped to C. Then she hopped to D.

But then she got stuck. She saw L, N, O and P. Where did M go? Brooklyn felt a little bad. She wanted M for her teddy's tag.

Then Dad began to hum a tune. Brooklyn knew that tune. It was the alphabet song. She sang along. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She kept singing. "H, I, J, K." Then she sang, "L, M, N, O, P."

The song put M after L! Brooklyn looked at the rug. She pointed to the spot right after L. "M goes here," she said. There it was, between L and N.

"M says mmm," said Dad. Brooklyn hugged her teddy. "M is for Moon," she said, pointing at a book about the moon. The moon could shine in the sky. Dad checked out the book for her.

Brooklyn waved to the letters. "Bye, A. Bye, B. Bye, M," she said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emile wants to read the book about the red truck. He finds it on the shelf. It is a thick book with a big flag on the cover. Emile opens it at the back. He points at the words. He starts at the right side of the page. He slides his finger to the left. The words do not match the pictures. The dog is on the wrong page.

"What is wrong?" he asks.

"You started at the back," says Miss Ana. She turns the book around. She opens the front cover. "Start here, on the left." Emile puts his finger on the first word. He slides it to the right. Now the words go with the pictures. The red truck beeps. Emile smiles and turns to the next page.

"Beep, beep," he says.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Ava sat at the dinner table. She had a big bite of pasta. The dog sat by her chair. "No begging," said Daddy. The dog begged anyway. Ava laughed.

"Can I stay up late?" Ava asked. "Pleeease?" Mommy looked out at the stormy sky. "You can try," she said. Ava tried. She stayed up long past her bath. She stayed up past her pajamas. She stayed up past her story.

The next morning, Ava was slow to get dressed. Her socks took a long time. She was too tired to play. She yawned at breakfast. Her milk sat untouched. "Does milk come from a cow?" she asked, yawning again.

That night, Ava took her bath early. She put on her pajamas. She went to bed on time.

The next morning, Ava jumped up. She dressed fast. She ran to her toys. "I can play!" she said. "I slept, and now I can play!"

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story: Blake ran into Mia's house. Mia had a music box and a drum. "We can play a song!" said Mia. Mia's mom said, "I will count one, two, three, four. Then we all start singing together." Blake could not wait. She started singing right away. But Mia was still quiet. Blake had to stop. She had sung too soon! "Oops," said Blake. "I lose my spot when I go too fast." Mia giggled. Mia's mom smiled. "Let's try again," she said. "Wait for the count. It is easy. One, two, three, four!" This time Blake waited. One, two, three, four. Then both girls sang at the same time. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" They did not miss a word. Blake clapped her hands to the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Mia clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. Then Mia's dog barked on the last clap! The girls laughed and laughed. "Again!" said Blake. "One, two, three, four!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Felix wanted a bedtime story. Grandma was busy, so Grandpa said, "I will read it."

Grandpa sat down. He opened the book. He started at the front. He turned the pages one by one. Then Grandma came in. "My turn," she said. She opened the book too.

Felix listened hard. Grandpa had said, "The moon was very sleepy." Now Grandma said the very same words. "The moon was very sleepy." Felix tapped the page. "Grandma, you said it just like Grandpa!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "The words are right there."

"The pencil words say it?" asked Felix.

"The printed words," Grandma said with a smile.

Felix looked closely. The little black marks sat on the page. They did not wiggle. They did not run away. Could paper really talk? Felix pointed at one word. "What does this one say?"

Grandpa leaned close. "It says moon."

Felix looked out the window. The noisy wind blew outside. The real moon was up in the sky.

"It is in the book and in the sky!" said Felix.

Grandma turned to the last page. She read the end. Then Felix closed the book himself, front cover down, just right.

"Again," said Felix.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Florence went to the library with her dad. She found a big book about a little mouse. The mouse had soft gray fur in the pictures. Florence loved those pictures. She wanted to know who drew them.

"Who made this mouse?" she asked her dad.

"Let's look," said Dad. He opened the front of the book. "We start here," he said. Florence pointed at the little black marks. Dad moved his finger under them. "These are words," he said. "They tell the story." The words said a name. "This is the illustrator," said Dad. "An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book."

Florence turned the pages one by one. The mouse moved to a barn. Then the mouse found some cheese. The pictures came after each other, front to back. At the end, the mouse slept in a nest.

Florence hugged the book. "This mouse is special," she said. "I want to take her home."

Dad helped her check out the book. Florence held it tight all the way to the door. "Good night, little mouse," she whispered. "I will read you again tomorrow."

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. His paper had a big round pumpkin on it. But the paint jars had no orange. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. Hudson frowned at the jars.

Then he had an idea. He put a blob of red on his brush. He put a blob of yellow next to it. He mixed them with the brush. Round and round went the brush. The paint turned orange! Hudson gasped. "Mama, look! Orange!"

He painted his pumpkin all orange. He painted a green stem too. His bear sat on the chair beside him. Hudson held the bear up to see. "Nice pumpkin," said Mama with a smile. Hudson yawned a big yawn. Paint time had made him sleepy. He leaned his head on Mama's arm. "My pumpkin can sleep now," he said.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story: Isla went to the pharmacy with Dad. The shop smelled like cough drops. On a shelf Isla saw a little fox toy. It was soft and orange. Isla held the fox while Dad got his medicine. Her tummy made a growl. "Snack time soon," said Dad. Isla looked at her hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said. They looked clean and pale. Dad got soap and water from the sink by the counter. "Let's wash," he said. Isla rubbed the soap on her hands. It felt slippery and smelled like flowers. It was hard to wait, so they sang "Happy Birthday" two times. That made twenty seconds. Isla sang loud. The fox watched from the counter. Then the soap bubbles went down the drain. Isla held her hands up to the light. They shone. Then came a small surprise. Dad opened his bag and pulled out a banana. Isla took one bite. "Mmm," she said. "Wash again after the toilet too," said Dad. "Sing with me," said Isla. "Happy birthday to you."
